notes.title: Bedrock AgentCore: run agents in production
notes.gist: AgentCore is the managed platform that hosts, connects and watches AI agents, so you don't build that plumbing yourself.
points: Runtime: serverless, session-isolated hosting for agents built with any framework or model.
Gateway turns APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools that agents can call.
Memory keeps short-term chat context and long-term knowledge across sessions.
Identity plugs into existing IdPs such as Cognito or Okta for agent auth.
Policy, Observability and Evaluations add rules, tracing and quality checks.
notes.tip: Agents to production with little undifferentiated work points to AgentCore services. Hand-building agent hosting, tool wrappers and session isolation on EC2 is the over-built distractor.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U([User]) --> RT[AgentCore Runtime]
  RT --> MEM[Memory: short and long term]
  RT --> GW[Gateway: MCP tools]
  GW --> API[APIs and Lambda]
  RT --> ID[Identity: IdP tokens]
  RT --> OBS[Observability traces]

notes.title: RAG with Bedrock Knowledge Bases
notes.gist: A knowledge base finds the right chunks of your own documents and feeds them to the model, so answers use your data.
points: Ingest: documents are split into chunks, embedded as vectors, stored in a vector index.
Query: the question is embedded, similar chunks retrieved, then added to the prompt.
Managed KB: Bedrock runs ingestion, indexing and storage; customer-managed: you run the vector store.
Customer-managed vector stores include OpenSearch Serverless, Aurora and Neptune.
Answers can carry citations; reranking models improve which chunks come back.
notes.tip: Fresh, private or citable answers point to RAG, not fine-tuning. Fine-tuning changes style or behaviour; it does not keep facts current.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  D[(Documents in S3)] --> C[Chunk]
  C --> E[Embed into vectors]
  E --> VX[(Vector index)]
  Q([User question]) --> R[Retrieve similar chunks]
  VX --> R
  R --> P[Prompt + retrieved context]
  P --> M[Model answer with citations]

notes.title: VPC Lattice for service-to-service networking
notes.gist: Lattice lets services in many VPCs and accounts call each other by name, with auth, and without peering or Transit Gateway.
points: Service network: a logical boundary of VPCs and services, shared across accounts with RAM.
Targets: EC2, IP addresses, Lambda, ALB, ECS tasks and Kubernetes pods.
Overlapping CIDRs are supported, which peering and Transit Gateway cannot handle.
Auth policies at service network and service level give IAM-based, fine-grained access.
Resource configurations share RDS or IP endpoints; on-premises connects via a service-network endpoint.
notes.tip: Many accounts, overlapping CIDRs and app-layer auth between microservices: choose Lattice. Transit Gateway is layer 3 routing between whole networks.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[Client VPC, account A] --> SN{{Service network}}
  B[Client VPC, account B] --> SN
  SN --> AP[Auth policy check]
  AP --> S1[Orders service on ECS]
  AP --> S2[Billing service on Lambda]
  AP --> RC[(RDS via resource configuration)]

notes.title: ECS Service Connect: short names, built-in mesh
notes.gist: Service Connect lets ECS services find and call each other by short names, with a managed proxy in every task.
points: Configured in the ECS service and task definition; no separate mesh to run.
Discovery uses an AWS Cloud Map namespace; names must be unique per namespace.
Proxy container per task: round-robin load balancing plus outlier detection.
Port name in the task definition; client alias sets the DNS name and port.
ECS only; use VPC Lattice when calls span EC2, Lambda, EKS or accounts.
notes.tip: ECS-only microservices needing discovery without extra infrastructure: Service Connect. Cross-account calls or mixed compute types point to VPC Lattice instead.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C[Client task] --> PX[Service Connect proxy]
  PX --> NS[Cloud Map namespace]
  PX --> T1[Server task, AZ a]
  PX --> T2[Server task, AZ b]
  PX -.-> CW[CloudWatch metrics]

notes.title: Decouple with EventBridge buses and pipes
notes.gist: Producers emit events to a bus; rules filter and route them to many targets, so services never call each other directly.
points: Event buses: many sources to many targets, with filtering and optional transformation.
Pipes: point-to-point from one source, such as a DynamoDB stream, to one target.
Scheduler runs cron and rate tasks centrally, replacing cron servers.
Custom buses can retain events and replay them.
Put SQS in front of a slow consumer to buffer bursts.
notes.tip: Fan-out with content filtering to many consumers: EventBridge. Smoothing bursts to one slow worker: SQS. Chains of synchronous API calls are the coupling trap.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P1[Orders service] --> BUS{{Event bus}}
  P2[SaaS partner events] --> BUS
  BUS -->|rule: type=paid| L[Lambda: invoice]
  BUS -->|rule: amount over 1000| SF[Step Functions: review]
  BUS --> Q[SQS: analytics buffer]

notes.title: Step Functions: Standard vs Express
notes.gist: Step Functions runs multi-step workflows as a state machine; pick Standard for long, exact runs and Express for fast, high-volume ones.
points: Standard: up to one year, exactly-once, priced per state transition.
Express: up to five minutes, at-least-once when async, priced by executions, duration, memory.
Standard suits non-idempotent steps like payments; Express suits idempotent stream processing.
Express lacks `.sync` and `.waitForTaskToken` patterns, Distributed Map and activities.
The workflow type cannot be changed after creation.
notes.tip: Human approval, long waits or payments mean Standard. IoT or streaming at huge rates means Express. Watch for any step longer than five minutes.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  S{Workflow need?} -->|over 5 min or human wait| STD[Standard: exactly-once]
  S -->|high volume, short| EXP[Express: at-least-once]
  STD --> P1[Payments, EMR jobs, approvals]
  EXP --> P2[IoT ingest, stream transforms]

notes.title: Transit Gateway and Direct Connect hub
notes.gist: Transit Gateway is a regional router that connects many VPCs and on-premises links through one hub instead of a peering mesh.
points: Attach VPCs, Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect gateways, Connect attachments and peered TGWs.
Separate route tables isolate groups such as prod and dev; blackhole routes drop traffic.
Transit gateway peering, including across Regions, uses static routes only.
Direct Connect VIFs: private to a VPC, public to AWS services, transit to TGW.
Enable appliance mode for stateful firewalls so a flow keeps the same AZ.
notes.tip: Dozens of VPCs plus on-premises: TGW with a Direct Connect gateway. Full-mesh peering does not scale and is not transitive. Site-to-Site VPN is the cheap backup path.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  DC[On-premises data centre] -->|Direct Connect| DXG[DX gateway]
  DXG -->|transit VIF| TGW{{Transit Gateway}}
  DC -.->|VPN backup| TGW
  TGW --> P[Prod VPCs route table]
  TGW --> DV[Dev VPCs route table]
  TGW --> SH[Shared services VPC]

summary.tests: Choosing the right managed building blocks for agents, RAG, service networking, event-driven integration, workflows and hybrid connectivity.
must_know: AgentCore hosts agents; Gateway turns APIs into MCP tools; Memory keeps context.
RAG with Knowledge Bases keeps answers current and citable; fine-tuning does not.
VPC Lattice: app-layer service networking across accounts, overlapping CIDRs, IAM auth policies.
Service Connect: ECS-only discovery and proxy through a Cloud Map namespace.
EventBridge fans out filtered events; SQS buffers work for one consumer.
Step Functions Standard: one year, exactly-once; Express: five minutes, at-least-once.
Transit Gateway is the hub for many VPCs, VPNs and Direct Connect.
traps: Using Transit Gateway or peering when overlapping CIDRs and service-level auth point to Lattice.
Choosing Express workflows for long waits, human approval or non-idempotent payment steps.
Fine-tuning a model to keep facts fresh instead of using RAG.

notes.title: SCPs and RCPs: org-wide permission ceilings
notes.gist: SCPs cap what your own users and roles can do; RCPs cap what anyone can do to your resources. Neither grants access.
points: SCP: limits IAM principals in member accounts, including root; never the management account.
RCP: limits access to resources, including by principals outside the organization.
Effective access is the intersection of SCPs, RCPs, identity and resource policies.
SCPs skip service-linked roles; attach at most 10 SCPs and 5 RCPs per target.
Test on a sandbox OU first; never remove `FullAWSAccess` without a replacement allow.
notes.tip: Stop outside accounts reaching your S3 buckets org-wide: RCP. Stop your developers using a Region: SCP. Any answer where an SCP grants access is wrong.

notes.title: Control Tower landing zone and controls
notes.gist: Control Tower builds a best-practice multi-account setup for you and keeps it governed with ready-made controls.
points: Orchestrates Organizations, IAM Identity Center and Service Catalog to build the landing zone.
Controls are preventive, detective or proactive; mandatory, strongly recommended or elective.
Account Factory vends new accounts from approved, preconfigured templates.
Dashboard shows noncompliant resources by account and OU; drift detection flags changes.
Existing organizations can be registered and existing accounts enrolled.
notes.tip: Many accounts, fast governed setup, least effort: Control Tower. Hand-building Organizations plus custom scripts is the high-effort distractor unless heavy customisation is required.

notes.title: Security Hub: one pane for findings
notes.gist: Security Hub gathers security findings from many accounts and tools into one place and scores you against standards.
points: Standards: AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS, PCI DSS and NIST.
Ingests GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and partner findings in the ASFF format.
Consolidates findings across accounts; an aggregation Region gives one cross-Region view.
Automation rules update or suppress findings; EventBridge triggers remediation.
Collects only findings created after you enable it; nothing retroactive.
notes.tip: Central compliance view across accounts means Security Hub. GuardDuty detects threats, Inspector finds vulnerabilities, Macie finds S3 PII; they feed Security Hub, not replace it.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  GD[GuardDuty threats] --> SH{{Security Hub}}
  IN[Inspector vulnerabilities] --> SH
  MA[Macie S3 PII] --> SH
  CK[Control checks: FSBP, CIS] --> SH
  SH --> EB[EventBridge rule]
  EB --> FIX[Automated remediation]

notes.title: Bedrock Guardrails for safe GenAI
notes.gist: Guardrails screen prompts and model answers for harmful content, banned topics, PII and hallucinations before users see them.
points: Filters: content, denied topics, words, sensitive information, contextual grounding, Automated Reasoning.
Sensitive information filters block or mask PII, including custom regex patterns.
Contextual grounding checks flag RAG answers not supported by the retrieved sources.
Attach by guardrail ID and version at inference, or call `ApplyGuardrail` without a model.
Organizations Bedrock policies can enforce guardrails across accounts.
notes.tip: Redact PII, block off-topic advice or catch hallucinations in a GenAI app: Guardrails. Prompt wording alone is the weak distractor; it is not an enforced control.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  U([User prompt]) --> G1[Guardrail: input check]
  G1 -->|blocked| MSG[Configured blocked message]
  G1 -->|ok| FM[Foundation model]
  FM --> G2[Guardrail: output check]
  G2 -->|violates| MSG
  G2 -->|PII masked, grounded| OUT([Safe answer])

notes.title: KMS post-quantum: ML-KEM and ML-DSA
notes.gist: AWS KMS adds quantum-resistant options: hybrid ML-KEM TLS to protect traffic, and ML-DSA keys for digital signatures.
points: Hybrid TLS combines ECDH with ML-KEM, NIST FIPS 203, on all KMS endpoints.
It defends long-lived secrets against harvest now, decrypt later attacks.
Hybrid TLS protects data in transit only; KMS key encryption is unchanged.
ML-DSA keys, FIPS 204, sign and verify: `ML_DSA_44`, `ML_DSA_65`, `ML_DSA_87`.
Confirm in CloudTrail `tlsDetails.keyExchange`, for example `X25519MLKEM768`.
notes.tip: Long-term secrets sent over TLS against future quantum attackers: enable hybrid post-quantum TLS in the SDK. Quantum-safe signing: an ML-DSA KMS key. Don't mix them up.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  APP[App with AWS SDK] -->|hybrid TLS: ECDH + ML-KEM| KMS[AWS KMS endpoint]
  KMS --> CT[CloudTrail: keyExchange field]
  PIPE[Release pipeline] -->|Sign| MLD[ML-DSA key in KMS]
  MLD --> VER[Verify signature]

source.title: Using hybrid post-quantum TLS with AWS KMS

notes.title: Clean Rooms: analyse shared data privately
notes.gist: Clean Rooms lets partners run approved queries across combined datasets without either side seeing the other's raw rows.
points: Create a collaboration, invite accounts, link configured tables; data stays where it is.
Analysis rules restrict which SQL can run and what output is allowed.
Differential privacy adds mathematical protection against re-identifying individuals.
Cryptographic computing keeps data encrypted even while queries run.
Clean Rooms ML finds lookalike users without sharing the training data.
notes.tip: Two companies must match customers or measure campaigns without exchanging raw data: Clean Rooms. Copying data into a shared S3 bucket breaks the privacy requirement.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  A[(Advertiser data in S3)] --> COL{{Clean Rooms collaboration}}
  B[(Publisher data in S3)] --> COL
  COL --> AR[Analysis rules + differential privacy]
  AR --> OUT[Aggregated results only]
  COL -.-> LOG[Analysis logs for audit]

summary.tests: Governing many accounts with preventive and detective controls, central findings, and protecting data and GenAI workloads.
must_know: SCPs and RCPs only cap permissions; they never grant access.
SCPs limit your principals; RCPs limit access to your resources, including by outsiders.
Neither SCPs nor RCPs affect the management account.
Control Tower builds the landing zone; Account Factory vends governed accounts.
Security Hub aggregates GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie findings and checks standards.
Guardrails filter content, mask PII and check grounding for Bedrock apps.
Hybrid ML-KEM TLS protects KMS traffic; ML-DSA keys give post-quantum signatures.
traps: Expecting an SCP to grant a permission, or to restrict the management account.
Picking GuardDuty or Macie when the need is a central compliance score across accounts.
Copying raw data into a shared bucket when Clean Rooms keeps rows private.

notes.title: Savings Plans: commit dollars per hour
notes.gist: Commit to a steady hourly spend for one or three years and AWS discounts matching usage automatically.
points: Compute SP: up to 66% off; any family, size, Region, OS; covers Fargate and Lambda.
EC2 Instance SP: up to 72% off; locked to one family in one Region.
Database SP: up to 35% off across Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB and more.
Pay all, partial or no upfront; terms cannot change after purchase.
Cost Explorer recommends the commitment level from your usage history.
notes.tip: Steady baseline that may change family or Region, or move to Fargate: Compute SP. Fixed family, biggest discount: EC2 Instance SP. Spot usage is never covered.

notes.title: Spot Instances for interruptible work
notes.gist: Spot sells spare EC2 capacity at steep discounts, but AWS can take it back with a two-minute warning.
points: Fits batch jobs, data analysis, background processing and other flexible, fault-tolerant work.
Interruption notice is two minutes; a rebalance recommendation can warn earlier.
Price is set per instance type and AZ from long-term supply and demand.
Spot is not covered by Savings Plans and doesn't count toward commitments.
Spread across instance types and AZs so losing one capacity pool hurts less.
notes.tip: Cheapest for stateless, retry-safe work: Spot. Never pick Spot alone for a database or a job that cannot be interrupted; keep an On-Demand or Savings Plan baseline.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR

  F -->|yes| SP[Spot: many types and AZs]

notes.title: Pick the right S3 storage class
notes.gist: Match each dataset's access pattern to a storage class; colder classes cost less to store but more to read.
points: Standard-IA and One Zone-IA: 30-day minimum, 128 KB minimum billed size, retrieval fee.
One Zone-IA lives in one AZ: only for re-creatable data or CRR replicas.
Glacier Instant Retrieval: millisecond reads, 90-day minimum, for roughly quarterly access.
Glacier Flexible: minutes to hours, 90 days; Deep Archive: hours, 180 days.
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects after 30 and 90 idle days; under 128 KB never tiers.
notes.tip: Unpredictable access: Intelligent-Tiering. Rare access but instant reads: Glacier Instant Retrieval. One Zone-IA for the only copy of irreplaceable data is the classic trap.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  D([Data]) --> A{Access pattern?}
  A -->|frequent| STD[S3 Standard]
  A -->|unknown or changing| IT[Intelligent-Tiering]
  A -->|monthly, ms reads| IA[Standard-IA]
  A -->|quarterly, ms reads| GIR[Glacier Instant Retrieval]
  A -->|yearly, can wait hours| GDA[Glacier Flexible or Deep Archive]

notes.title: S3 Lifecycle rules automate tiering
notes.gist: Lifecycle rules move ageing objects to cheaper classes and delete them when no longer needed, with no code.
points: Transition actions change the storage class; expiration actions delete objects.
Rules apply to existing objects as well as new uploads.
Transitions are billed per request; weigh that for millions of small objects.
Expiring before a class's minimum storage duration still charges that minimum.
Bucket policies cannot block lifecycle deletions or transitions.
notes.tip: Known ageing pattern, like logs hot for 30 days then archived: lifecycle rules. Unknown pattern: Intelligent-Tiering. A Lambda that moves objects is the over-built answer.

flowchart LR
  UP([Upload]) --> S[Standard: days 0 to 30]
  S -->|day 30| IA[Standard-IA]
  IA -->|day 90| GF[Glacier Flexible Retrieval]
  GF -->|day 365| EXP[Expire: delete]

notes.title: Cut data transfer costs
notes.gist: Data moving through NAT, across Regions and out to the internet costs money, so design short, private paths.
points: Gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB have no hourly charge and skip NAT.
Interface endpoints via PrivateLink have an hourly fee but avoid public paths.
Place NAT gateways in the same AZ as the high-traffic instances.
CloudFront caches at edge locations, cutting origin load and transfer.
Direct Connect can cut network cost versus internet links; Snow devices move petabytes offline.
notes.tip: EC2 pulling lots of S3 data through a NAT gateway: add an S3 gateway endpoint, which has no hourly charge. This is the most common cost fix tested.

  EC2 ==>|cheaper path| GWE[S3 gateway endpoint]

  U([Global users]) --> CF[CloudFront edge cache]

notes.title: Cost visibility, tags and rightsizing
notes.gist: You can't cut what you can't see: tag resources, track spend per team, then rightsize using real utilisation data.
points: Cost allocation tags must be activated in Billing before they appear in reports.
Only the management account manages cost allocation tags for an organization.
Compute Optimizer reads 14 days of CloudWatch metrics to suggest sizes and spot idle resources.
It covers EC2, Auto Scaling groups, EBS, Lambda, Fargate, RDS, NAT gateways and more.
Opt in first; opt in the management account for organization-wide recommendations.
notes.tip: Chargeback per team or project: activated cost allocation tags plus Cost Explorer. Oversized fleet: Compute Optimizer. Forgetting to activate tags is the common gap.

notes.title: RTO and RPO set the design
notes.gist: RTO is how long you can be down; RPO is how much recent data you can lose. Both come from business impact.
points: RTO: maximum acceptable time from interruption to restored service.
RPO: maximum acceptable time since the last recovery point.
A business impact analysis sets targets per workload; impact can vary by date.
Backup frequency sets the achievable RPO; redeploy speed sets the RTO.
Don't spend more on recovery than the outage would cost, unless regulation requires it.
notes.tip: Read the numbers first: minutes of RPO rule out nightly backups; minutes of RTO rule out rebuilding from backups. Then pick the cheapest strategy that fits.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  LP[Last recovery point] -->|RPO: data you may lose| X{{Disaster}}
  X -->|RTO: downtime allowed| BK[Service restored]
  BIA[Business impact analysis] -.-> LP
  BIA -.-> BK

source.title: Business Continuity Plan (BCP) - Disaster Recovery of Workloads on AWS

notes.title: Four DR strategies, cost versus speed
notes.gist: DR runs from cheap, slow backups to costly active-active; each step up keeps more of the stack running elsewhere.
points: Backup and restore: data backed up, infrastructure redeployed by IaC; highest RTO.
Pilot light: data replicated live, core infrastructure ready but app servers off.
Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully working copy that can take traffic at once.
Active-active: every Region serves traffic; async replication gives near-zero RPO.
Fail over with data plane actions; avoid depending on control plane calls.
notes.tip: Pilot light versus warm standby is the classic trap: pilot light cannot serve requests until scaled up; warm standby serves immediately at reduced capacity.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  B[Backup and restore: lowest cost] --> PL[Pilot light: data live, app off]
  PL --> WS[Warm standby: small live copy]
  WS --> AA[Active-active: all Regions serve]
  AA --> R[Lower RTO and RPO, higher cost]

notes.title: Resilience Hub: check RTO and RPO
notes.gist: Resilience Hub checks whether an app's design can meet its RTO and RPO goals and tells you what to fix.
points: Set goals in a resiliency policy, then assess the application against them.
Recommendations follow the AWS Well-Architected Framework.
Create and run Fault Injection Service experiments from the hub.
Works alongside AWS Backup, Elastic Disaster Recovery and ARC.
Run assessments regularly to keep tracking whether targets are still met.
notes.tip: A question asking to continuously validate that workloads still meet RTO and RPO targets points to Resilience Hub, not a one-off manual architecture review.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  POL[Resiliency policy: RTO, RPO targets] --> ASM[Assess application]
  APP[(Application resources)] --> ASM
  ASM --> REC[Recommendations to close gaps]
  REC --> FIS[Run FIS experiments]
  FIS --> ASM

notes.title: Fault Injection Service chaos experiments
notes.gist: FIS breaks things on purpose, in a controlled way, so you learn how the system fails before a real outage does.
points: Experiment template = actions + targets + stop conditions.
Targets are chosen by resource ID or by tags and state.
Stop conditions are CloudWatch alarms that halt the experiment automatically.
Actions run in sequence or in parallel; multi-account experiments are supported.
FIS takes real actions on real resources; rehearse in pre-production first.
notes.tip: Prove the app survives instance or AZ loss with safety guardrails: FIS with alarm stop conditions. Home-made scripts that terminate instances lack those controls.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  T[Experiment template] --> A[Actions: stop instances, add latency]
  T --> TG[Targets: by tag]
  T --> SC[Stop condition: CloudWatch alarm]
  A --> RUN[Run experiment]
  TG --> RUN
  RUN --> OBS[Observe and fix weaknesses]
  SC -.->|alarm fires| HALT[Experiment stopped]

notes.title: ARC: zonal shift and Region failover
notes.gist: Application Recovery Controller moves traffic away from a sick AZ or Region quickly and safely.
points: Zonal shift: manual, temporary move away from one AZ, expiry up to three days.
Zonal autoshift: AWS shifts traffic for you when its telemetry sees an AZ impairment.
Routing control: highly reliable DNS failover between Regions, with safety rules.
Region switch: orchestrated multi-Region recovery plans across accounts.
Readiness check watches quotas, capacity and routing so the standby can take load.
notes.tip: Gray failure or a bad deploy in one AZ: zonal shift. Controlled Region failover: routing control or Region switch, not hand-edited DNS records.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  IMP{Impairment scope?} -->|one AZ| ZS[Zonal shift or autoshift]
  ZS --> HAZ[Healthy AZs, same Region]
  IMP -->|whole Region| RC[Routing control or Region switch]
  RC --> R2[Standby Region]
  RDY[Readiness check] -.-> R2

notes.title: The 7 Rs migration strategies
notes.gist: Each app gets one of seven moves, from shutting it down to rebuilding it cloud-native, based on value, risk and effort.
points: Retire switches the app off; retain keeps it where it is for now.
Rehost is lift and shift; relocate moves to a cloud version of the same platform.
Replatform makes small tweaks, such as SQL Server to Amazon RDS.
Repurchase swaps the app for SaaS: drop and shop.
Refactor re-architects cloud-native; most complex, so avoid it during large migrations.
notes.tip: Fastest with least change: rehost. Managed database with little code change: replatform. Big agility goals: refactor. Large migrations should move first and modernise later.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  APP([Application]) --> NV{Still needed?}
  NV -->|no| RET[Retire]
  NV -->|not yet| RTN[Retain]
  NV -->|yes| C{How much change?}
  C -->|none| RH[Rehost or relocate]
  C -->|small| RP[Replatform]
  C -->|replace with SaaS| RPU[Repurchase]
  C -->|redesign| RF[Refactor]

notes.title: Migration tools: MGN, DMS, DataSync
notes.gist: Pick the tool by what you are moving: whole servers, databases, or files and objects.
points: MGN, now AWS Transform MGN: block-level server replication, cutover in minutes.
DMS: full load plus ongoing change replication keeps source and target in sync.
DMS Schema Conversion or AWS SCT converts schemas when the engine changes.
DataSync: online file and object transfer with encryption and integrity checks.
Migration Hub closed to new customers in November 2025; AWS Transform replaces it.
notes.tip: Rehost servers: MGN. Change database engine with little downtime: Schema Conversion plus DMS ongoing replication. Bulk files online: DataSync. Too little bandwidth: Snowball.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SRC([On-premises estate]) --> K{What is moving?}
  K -->|servers, VMs| MGN[AWS Transform MGN]
  K -->|databases| DMS[DMS + Schema Conversion]
  K -->|files and objects| DS[DataSync]
  K -->|petabytes, low bandwidth| SNOW[Snowball Edge]

summary.tests: Matching DR strategies to RTO and RPO, testing resilience, and choosing the right migration strategy and tool.
must_know: RTO is allowed downtime; RPO is allowed data loss, measured in time.
Backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active: rising cost, falling RTO.
Pilot light cannot serve traffic until scaled up; warm standby can at once.
Resilience Hub assesses apps against RTO and RPO targets; FIS injects real faults safely.
ARC zonal shift moves traffic off one AZ; routing control fails over Regions.
7 Rs: retire, retain, rehost, relocate, replatform, repurchase, refactor.
MGN for servers, DMS for databases, DataSync for files, Snowball for offline bulk.
traps: Confusing pilot light with warm standby when the RTO is minutes.
Refactoring during a large migration instead of rehosting first and modernising later.
Failing over with control plane actions instead of data plane switches.

notes.title: Security gates in the CI/CD pipeline
notes.gist: Build security checks into every pipeline stage so vulnerable code or images are stopped before they reach production.
points: ECR enhanced scanning uses Amazon Inspector for OS and language package CVEs.
Enhanced scanning runs on push and continuously; new findings emit EventBridge events.
Basic scanning covers OS packages only, on push or manually.
Fail the pipeline stage when findings exceed an agreed severity.
Well-Architected DevOps Guidance lists capabilities, metrics and anti-patterns to measure maturity.
notes.tip: Re-checking already pushed images as new CVEs appear needs ECR enhanced scanning with Inspector. Basic scan on push alone misses vulnerabilities published later.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SRC[Commit] --> BLD[Build and unit tests]
  BLD --> SAST[Code scan]
  SAST --> IMG[Push image to ECR]
  IMG --> SCAN{Critical Inspector findings?}
  SCAN -->|yes| STOP[Fail pipeline and notify]
  SCAN -->|no| DEP[Deploy]

notes.title: Blue/green, canary and linear deployments
notes.gist: Shift traffic to a new version gradually or all at once, and keep a fast way back if alarms fire.
points: In-place on EC2: AllAtOnce, HalfAtATime or OneAtATime, set by minimum healthy hosts.
Canary: 10% first, the rest after a wait, e.g. `LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes`.
Linear: equal steps, e.g. 10% every minute until all traffic moves.
ECS and Lambda deployments shift traffic to a new task set or function version.
With a Network Load Balancer, ECS supports only `ECSAllAtOnce`.
notes.tip: Least risk with quick rollback: blue/green or canary with alarm-based rollback. All-at-once in place is the fastest but riskiest distractor.

notes.title: Lakehouse governance: Lake Formation + Iceberg
notes.gist: Lake Formation is the single permission layer for your data lake; Iceberg tables add database-like updates on S3.
points: Fine-grained grants at database, table, column, row and cell level.
Tag-based access control, LF-TBAC, scales permissions with tags instead of per-table grants.
Manages permissions for open table formats: Apache Iceberg, Hudi and Delta Lake.
Shares data across accounts and organizations without copying it.
Hybrid access mode lets you adopt Lake Formation permissions gradually alongside IAM.
notes.tip: Column or row-level access for many analysts across accounts: Lake Formation. Juggling many S3 bucket policies and IAM rules is the high-effort wrong answer.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S3[(S3: Iceberg tables)] --> CAT[Glue Data Catalog]
  CAT --> LF{{Lake Formation permissions}}
  LF -->|columns, rows| ATH[Athena analysts]
  LF -->|tags| ETL[EMR or Glue jobs]
  LF -->|cross-account share| ACC2[Consumer account]

notes.title: CloudWatch observability: signals, synthetics, RUM
notes.gist: CloudWatch shows how the app behaves for real users and across accounts, not just whether servers are up.
points: Application Signals auto-collects call volume, latency, faults and errors; tracks SLOs.
It draws an application map; supports Java, Python, Node.js and .NET.
Synthetics canaries probe endpoints on a schedule; RUM measures real user sessions.
Cross-account observability links source accounts to a monitoring account, also via Organizations.
Alarms on metrics or SLOs can trigger notifications and automated runbooks.
notes.tip: Find problems before users report them: Synthetics canaries. Measure real user experience: RUM. One view across many accounts: cross-account observability, not log-copying scripts.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  RUM[RUM: real browsers] --> AS{{Application Signals}}
  SYN[Synthetics canaries] --> AS
  APP[Services on ECS, EKS, EC2] --> AS
  AS --> SLO[SLOs and application map]
  SRC[Source accounts] -->|link| MON[Monitoring account]
  AS --> MON

notes.title: Systems Manager Automation runbooks
notes.gist: Systems Manager runs fixes and routine tasks across fleets and accounts as repeatable runbooks, not manual logins.
points: Managed nodes need SSM Agent; no bastion hosts or SSH required.
Runbooks are AWS-provided or custom; `aws:executeScript` runs Python or PowerShell.
Rate controls set concurrency and error thresholds for safe bulk changes.
Run automations across multiple accounts and Regions from one place.
EventBridge can trigger runbooks, for example to remediate a compliance finding.
notes.tip: Auto-remediate drift or findings with least effort: EventBridge rule to an SSM Automation runbook. Custom Lambda scripts or manual SSH are the usual weaker options.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  FND[Config or Security Hub finding] --> EB[EventBridge rule]
  EB --> RB[SSM Automation runbook]
  RB -->|rate control| FLEET[Instances across accounts]
  RB --> LOG[CloudWatch Logs output]
  RB -->|approval step| OPS([Operator])

notes.title: StackSets: one template, many accounts
notes.gist: StackSets deploy the same CloudFormation stack to many accounts and Regions in one operation.
points: An administrator account owns the template; stack instances land in target accounts and Regions.
Service-managed permissions with Organizations can auto-deploy to new accounts in an OU.
Typical use: org baselines such as IAM roles, Config rules and logging.
Run StackSet changes from a pipeline so baselines are reviewed before rollout.
Also useful for DR: deploy identical infrastructure into a recovery Region.
notes.tip: Deploy a baseline to every current and future account automatically: StackSets with service-managed permissions and auto-deployment. Running scripts per account is the error-prone distractor.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  ADM[Administrator account] --> SS{{StackSet template}}
  SS --> OU1[OU: prod accounts]
  SS --> OU2[OU: dev accounts]
  OU1 --> R1[Stacks in two Regions]
  NEW([New account joins OU]) -.->|auto-deploy| SS

summary.tests: Automating deployments, security checks, monitoring and remediation across accounts with the least manual operations effort.
must_know: ECR enhanced scanning with Inspector re-scans images continuously as new CVEs appear.
CodeDeploy canary shifts 10% first; linear shifts equal steps; all-at-once is riskiest.
Lake Formation grants database, table, column, row and cell access; LF-TBAC scales it.
Application Signals, Synthetics and RUM cover service health, probes and real users.
Cross-account observability links source accounts to one monitoring account.
EventBridge rule to SSM Automation runbook is the standard auto-remediation path.
StackSets with service-managed permissions auto-deploy baselines to new OU accounts.
traps: Writing custom Lambda or SSH scripts where an SSM runbook or StackSet already fits.
Choosing all-at-once deployment when the question stresses minimal risk or fast rollback.
Managing many S3 bucket policies instead of Lake Formation fine-grained grants.
